title: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking
shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Search Order ...
summary: This sub-technique abuses the order in which Windows resolves a program name that is given without a full path. When one program starts another by name alone, the operating system checks a sequence of locations, and the directory of the calling program is commonly examined before the system directories. An attacker who notices that a trusted program launches a helper this way can drop a file with that name into the calling program's own folder, so the helper is silently replaced. The outcome also depends on the extension search order defined by the PATHEXT setting, which is why a file named net.com can win over net.exe for the same request. It differs from the PATH variable variant in that the attacker targets the resolution rules of the launching process rather than the global folder list, so the artefact is an unexpected executable sitting beside a legitimate one. Process creation records showing a parent launching a child from its own directory are the primary detection signal.

beginner.definition: Some programs start other programs without saying exactly where those files live. Windows then searches a fixed order of folders to find the name. This sub-technique places a file with the expected name in a folder searched early. The calling program then starts the wrong file, as in the Hijack Execution Flow parent.
beginner.whyItMatters: A trusted program can become the delivery method for malicious code. The event looks like normal parent and child activity inside one application folder. Attackers also use the extension order, so a different file type can win the same request. Finding this requires knowing where each helper should live. Compare the expected paths with the paths that actually ran.
howItWorks: A program starts a helper program by name, without a full folder path.
Windows searches several folders in a fixed order to find that name.
The folder of the calling program is usually checked before the system folders.
The attacker puts a file with the helper's name in that calling folder.
The extension order in the PATHEXT setting decides which file type wins.
The parent program then launches the attacker's file in place of the real one.
beginner.example: Imagine a clinic where a doctor asks an assistant to fetch a form. The assistant looks first in the room where they are standing, then in the main storeroom. Someone has left a fake form in that first room. The assistant brings it without checking the storeroom at all. Search order hijacking works like that. The program looks beside itself first and uses whatever it finds. The real file stays untouched in the system folder.
takeaways: A program that starts helpers by name trusts the folder it sits in.
The extension order setting also affects which file is chosen.
A child process running from its parent's folder can be suspicious.

objectives: Describe how Windows resolves a program name that is given without a full path.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the PATH environment variable variant.
Explain the role of the PATHEXT setting in choosing which file runs.
Identify process creation records that show parent and child program paths.
Describe which folders should be checked for unexpected executable files.
